description_full: Bunzl plc operates as a distribution and services company in the North America, Continental Europe, the United Kingdom, Ireland, and internationally. It provides personal protection and safety equipment, including gloves, boots, hard hats, ear and eye protection, other workwear, as well as cleaning and hygiene supplies and asset protection products; and healthcare consumables, such as gloves, masks, swabs, gowns, bandages, healthcare devices, and other healthcare related equipment. The company also offers cleaning and hygiene materials comprising chemicals and hygiene paper; goods-not-for-resale, including food packaging, films, labels, and other store supplies; non-food consumables, such as food packaging, disposable tableware, guest amenities, catering equipment, and agricultural supplies; and other products. It serves its products to industrial, construction, e-commerce, hospitals, care homes and other facilities serving the healthcare, public sector customers, grocery stores, supermarkets, convenience stores, hotels, restaurants, contract caterers, food processors, commercial growers, leisure, retail customers, and office supply companies. Bunzl plc was founded in 1854 and is based in London, the United Kingdom.
ceo_bio: Mr. Frank Andre Van Zanten M.B.A. | CEO & Executive Director | Age 58 | Compensation: $2.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 26K people. Revenue per employee of $584K ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $42K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $173 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 5× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Bunzl plc is a large-cap industrials business with a $11.9B market cap on $15.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 7% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.99× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.3×.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.6% over 3 years.

Analysts expect 2.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
